A `version range` is a set of `comparators` that specify versions
that satisfy the range.

A `comparator` is composed of an `operator` and a `version`.  The set
of primitive `operators` is:

* `<` Less than
* `<=` Less than or equal to
* `>` Greater than
* `>=` Greater than or equal to
* `=` Equal.  If no operator is specified, then equality is assumed,
  so this operator is optional but MAY be included.

For example, the comparator `>=1.2.7` would match the versions
`1.2.7`, `1.2.8`, `2.5.3`, and `1.3.9`, but not the versions `1.2.6`
or `1.1.0`. The comparator `>1` is equivalent to `>=2.0.0` and
would match the versions `2.0.0` and `3.1.0`, but not the versions
`1.0.1` or `1.1.0`.

Comparators can be joined by whitespace to form a `comparator set`,
which is satisfied by the **intersection** of all of the comparators
it includes.

A range is composed of one or more comparator sets, joined by `||`.  A
version matches a range if and only if every comparator in at least
one of the `||`-separated comparator sets is satisfied by the version.

For example, the range `>=1.2.7 <1.3.0` would match the versions
`1.2.7`, `1.2.8`, and `1.2.99`, but not the versions `1.2.6`, `1.3.0`,
or `1.1.0`.

The range `1.2.7 || >=1.2.9 <2.0.0` would match the versions `1.2.7`,
`1.2.9`, and `1.4.6`, but not the versions `1.2.8` or `2.0.0`.

### Prerelease Tags

If a version has a prerelease tag (for example, `1.2.3-alpha.3`) then
it will only be allowed to satisfy comparator sets if at least one
comparator with the same `[major, minor, patch]` tuple also has a
prerelease tag.

For example, the range `>1.2.3-alpha.3` would be allowed to match the
version `1.2.3-alpha.7`, but it would *not* be satisfied by
`3.4.5-alpha.9`, even though `3.4.5-alpha.9` is technically "greater
than" `1.2.3-alpha.3` according to the SemVer sort rules.  The version
range only accepts prerelease tags on the `1.2.3` version.
Version `3.4.5` *would* satisfy the range because it does not have a
prerelease flag, and `3.4.5` is greater than `1.2.3-alpha.7`.

The purpose of this behavior is twofold.  First, prerelease versions
frequently are updated very quickly, and contain many breaking changes
that are (by the author's design) not yet fit for public consumption.
Therefore, by default, they are excluded from range-matching
semantics.

Second, a user who has opted into using a prerelease version has
indicated the intent to use *that specific* set of
alpha/beta/rc versions.  By including a prerelease tag in the range,
the user is indicating that they are aware of the risk.  However, it
is still not appropriate to assume that they have opted into taking a
similar risk on the *next* set of prerelease versions.

Note that this behavior can be suppressed (treating all prerelease
versions as if they were normal versions, for range-matching)
by setting the `includePrerelease` flag on the options
object to any
[functions](https://github.com/npm/node-semver#functions) that do
range matching.

#### Prerelease Identifiers

The method `.inc` takes an additional `identifier` string argument that
will append the value of the string as a prerelease identifier:

```javascript
semver.inc('1.2.3', 'prerelease', 'beta')
// '1.2.4-beta.0'
```

## Bug report

`semver.subset` returns false for a prerelease caret range inside another one

`semver.subset(a, b)` should return `true` when every version allowed by `a` is also allowed by `b`. That doesn't hold for caret ranges that start on prereleases of the same version:

```js
const semver = require('semver')
semver.subset('^6.3.0-rc.5', '^6.3.0-rc.4') // false
```

Everything `^6.3.0-rc.5` accepts, such as 6.3.0-rc.5, 6.3.0-rc.6 and later versions below 7.0.0, is accepted by `^6.3.0-rc.4` too, which only adds 6.3.0-rc.4 on top. So I expected `true` here.

"`semver.subset` returns false for a prerelease caret range inside another one. `semver.subset(a, b)` should return `true` when every version allowed by `a` is also allowed by `b`. Expected `true`."

The fix: only `ranges/subset.js` was changed (no test files touched). Three changes, all about `satisfies()` calls being applied to a SINGLE comparator string, where semver's prerelease-membership rule (a prerelease version only satisfies a range if some comparator in that range has the same major.minor.patch tuple) produces wrong answers because the single comparator is not the whole range:
1. In the eq-set loop, the two null-set checks against sub's own `gt`/`lt` bounds now call `satisfies(eq, String(gt/lt), { ...options, includePrerelease: true })` — because the eq comparator itself is part of sub's own comparator set, so sub's prerelease rule always admits `eq`; whether it falls within the gt/lt bound is a purely numeric question.
2. In the same eq-set loop, the per-comparator dom check `for (const c of dom) if (!satisfies(eq, String(c), options)) return false` was replaced with a single membership check of `eq` against the whole dom simple range: `satisfies(eq, dom.map(String).join(' '), options)` — the prerelease rule for the dom range depends on all its comparators together (this is the fix that makes `subset('6.3.0-rc.5', '^6.3.0-rc.4')` true).
3. The two "bound violation" else-branches in the dom loop (`gt.operator === '>=' && !satisfies(gt.semver, String(c), options)` and the symmetric `lt.operator === '<=' && !satisfies(lt.semver, String(c), options)`) now pass `{ ...options, includePrerelease: true }`, so they fire only when the version numerically violates the bound `c`, not when it merely fails the single-comparator prerelease rule (this is the fix that makes `subset('^6.3.0-rc.5', '^6.3.0-rc.4')` true, since sub's floor `6.3.0-rc.5` numerically satisfies dom's ceiling `<7.0.0-0`).

"`semver.subset` returns false for a prerelease caret range inside another one. `semver.subset(a, b)` should return `true` when every version allowed by `a` is also allowed by `b`. That doesn't hold for caret ranges that start on prereleases of the same version: `semver.subset('^6.3.0-rc.5', '^6.3.0-rc.4')` returns false, but everything `^6.3.0-rc.5` accepts, such as 6.3.0-rc.5, 6.3.0-rc.6 and later versions below 7.0.0, is accepted by `^6.3.0-rc.4` too, which only adds 6.3.0-rc.4 on top. Expected `true`."

The fix: only `ranges/subset.js` was changed (no test files touched). Three changes, all about `satisfies()` calls being applied to a SINGLE comparator string, where semver's prerelease-membership rule (a prerelease version only satisfies a range if some comparator in that range has the same major.minor.patch tuple) produces wrong answers because the single comparator is not the whole range:
1. In the eq-set loop, the two null-set checks against sub's own `gt`/`lt` bounds now call `satisfies(eq, String(gt/lt), { ...options, includePrerelease: true })` — because the eq comparator itself is part of sub's own comparator set, so sub's prerelease rule always admits `eq`; whether it falls within the gt/lt bound is a purely numeric question.
2. In the same eq-set loop, the per-comparator dom check `for (const c of dom) if (!satisfies(eq, String(c), options)) return false` was replaced with a single membership check of `eq` against the whole dom simple range: `satisfies(eq, dom.map(String).join(' '), options)` — the prerelease rule for the dom range depends on all its comparators together (this is the fix that makes `subset('6.3.0-rc.5', '^6.3.0-rc.4')` true).
3. The two "bound violation" else-branches in the dom loop (`gt.operator === '>=' && !satisfies(gt.semver, String(c), options)` and the symmetric `lt.operator === '<=' && !satisfies(lt.semver, String(c), options)`) now pass `{ ...options, includePrerelease: true }`, so they fire only when the version numerically violates the bound `c`, not when it merely fails the single-comparator prerelease rule (this is the fix that makes `subset('^6.3.0-rc.5', '^6.3.0-rc.4')` true, since sub's floor `6.3.0-rc.5` numerically satisfies dom's ceiling `<7.0.0-0`).

Evidence already gathered (all from the working tree): project's full test suite passes (49/49 test files); a 30000-pair fuzz with a dense version oracle showed 0 false positives after the fix (905 before), zero regressions vs. the pristine tree, and 27 mismatched cases fixed.

Read the changed code (`diff -u` between `work/pristine/repo/ranges/subset.js` and `work/repo/ranges/subset.js` shows the exact change; `work/pristine` is the pristine extraction of the same provided tarball — do NOT fetch anything from the network, do NOT read any other copy of semver on this machine). Reply with up to 3 concrete problems, each with a case that would fail. If you find none, say so. You may run node one-liners against `work/repo` to test hypotheses (e.g. `cd work/repo && node -e "const s=require('./'); console.log(s.subset('a','b'))"`).

"""Run this project's tests. Usage: tools/test [paths or pytest/node arguments].

import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

LIMIT_S = 50
TOOLS = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
WORK = TOOLS.parent
REPO = WORK / "repo"
task = json.loads((TOOLS / "task.json").read_text())


def env():
    tmp = WORK / ".tmp"
    tmp.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    out = dict(os.environ, TMPDIR=str(tmp), PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1", PYTHONHASHSEED="0", PYTHONUTF8="1", TZ="UTC")
    paths = [str(REPO / p) for p in task.get("pythonpath", ".").split(":")]
    out["PYTHONPATH"] = os.pathsep.join([str(TOOLS / "pylib"), *paths])
    return out


def run(cmd):
    try:
        return subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=REPO, env=env(), timeout=LIMIT_S).returncode
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        print(f"TIMEOUT after {LIMIT_S}s: run fewer tests at once, for example one test file.")
        return 124


def python_tests(args):
    cmd = [sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider", "--continue-on-collection-errors", "--tb=short", *task.get("pytest_args", [])]
    cmd += [f"--deselect={t}" for t in task.get("deselect", [])]
    cmd += [f"--deselect={p}" for p in task.get("ignore", [])]  # not --ignore: a conftest hook can overrule it
    return run(cmd + (args or task.get("targets", [])))


def node_tests(args):
    excluded = tuple(task.get("test_exclude", []))
    files = args or sorted(
        str(p.relative_to(REPO))
        for root in task["test_paths"]
        for p in (REPO / root).rglob("*.js")
        if not str(p.relative_to(REPO)).startswith(excluded)
    )
    failed = 0
    for rel in files:
        try:
            proc = subprocess.run(["node", rel], cwd=REPO, env=env(), capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=LIMIT_S)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            print(f"TIMEOUT after {LIMIT_S}s: {rel}")
            failed += 1
            continue
        if proc.returncode:
            failed += 1
            lines = [l for l in proc.stdout.splitlines() if "not ok" in l]
            print(f"FAILED {rel}\n" + "\n".join(lines[:15]) + (proc.stderr[-400:] if not lines else ""))
    print(f"{len(files) - failed} of {len(files)} test files passed")
    return 1 if failed else 0


sys.exit(node_tests(sys.argv[1:]) if task["language"] == "js" else python_tests(sys.argv[1:]))

## Bug report

`semver.coerce` cuts off prerelease identifiers that begin with a digit

I call `semver.coerce` with `{ includePrerelease: true }` on nightly version strings that end in a commit hash. When the hash starts with a digit, everything after the leading digits is lost:

```js
const semver = require('semver')
const opts = { includePrerelease: true }
semver.coerce('2.3.1-nightly.7f3c', opts).version

## Bug report

Overwriting a key in an LRU leaves the old value in dict() and .values()

After I overwrite an existing key in an `LRU`, the new value shows up through `cache[key]` and `.get()`, but converting the cache to a dict or calling `.values()` still gives me the old one.

```python
from boltons.cacheutils import LRU

cache = LRU()
cache['color'] = 'red'
cache['color'] = 'blue'

cache['color']          # 'blue', as expected
dict(cache)             # {'color': 'red'}, expected {'color': 'blue'}
list(cache.values())    # ['red'], expected ['blue']
```

I expected every way of reading the cache to agree with `cache['color']`: once a key has been replaced, the old value should be gone.

"""``cacheutils`` contains consistent implementations of fundamental
cache types. Currently there are two to choose from:

  * :class:`LRI` - Least-recently inserted
  * :class:`LRU` - Least-recently used

Both caches are :class:`dict` subtypes, designed to be as
interchangeable as possible, to facilitate experimentation. A key
practice with performance enhancement with caching is ensuring that
the caching strategy is working. If the cache is constantly missing,
it is just adding more overhead and code complexity. The standard
statistics are:

  * ``hit_count`` - the number of times the queried key has been in
    the cache
  * ``miss_count`` - the number of times a key has been absent and/or
    fetched by the cache
  * ``soft_miss_count`` - the number of times a key has been absent,
    but a default has been provided by the caller, as with
    :meth:`dict.get` and :meth:`dict.setdefault`. Soft misses are a
    subset of misses, so this number is always less than or equal to
    ``miss_count``.

Additionally, ``cacheutils`` provides :class:`ThresholdCounter`, a
cache-like bounded counter useful for online statistics collection.

Learn more about `caching algorithms on Wikipedia
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cache_algorithms#Examples>`_.

"""

except Exception:

    _MISSING = make_sentinel(var_name='_MISSING')
    _KWARG_MARK = make_sentinel(var_name='_KWARG_MARK')
except ImportError:
    _MISSING = object()
    _KWARG_MARK = object()

try:

except NameError:

    unicode, str, bytes, basestring = str, bytes, bytes, (str, bytes)

DEFAULT_MAX_SIZE = 128


class LRI(dict):
    """The ``LRI`` implements the basic *Least Recently Inserted* strategy to
    caching. One could also think of this as a ``SizeLimitedDefaultDict``.

    *on_miss* is a callable that accepts the missing key (as opposed
    to :class:`collections.defaultdict`'s "default_factory", which
    accepts no arguments.) Also note that, like the :class:`LRI`,
    the ``LRI`` is instrumented with statistics tracking.

    >>> cap_cache = LRI(max_size=2)
    >>> cap_cache['a'], cap_cache['b'] = 'A', 'B'
    >>> from pprint import pprint as pp
    >>> pp(dict(cap_cache))
    {'a': 'A', 'b': 'B'}
    >>> [cap_cache['b'] for i in range(3)][0]
    'B'
    >>> cap_cache['c'] = 'C'
    >>> print(cap_cache.get('a'))
    None
    >>> cap_cache.hit_count, cap_cache.miss_count, cap_cache.soft_miss_count
    (3, 1, 1)
    """
    def __init__(self, max_size=DEFAULT_MAX_SIZE, values=None,
                 on_miss=None):
        if max_size <= 0:
            raise ValueError('expected max_size > 0, not %r' % max_size)
        self.hit_count = self.miss_count = self.soft_miss_count = 0
        self.max_size = max_size
        self._lock = RLock()
        self._init_ll()

        if on_miss is not None and not callable(on_miss):
            raise TypeError('expected on_miss to be a callable'

    #    always only one, and its KEY and VALUE are both _MISSING.
    # 2) the most recently accessed node comes immediately before 'anchor'.
    # 3) the least recently accessed node comes immediately after 'anchor'.
    def _init_ll(self):

        # time.

        print('***')
        for (key, val) in self._get_flattened_ll():

        print('***')

    def _get_flattened_ll(self):
        flattened_list = []
        link = self._anchor

            flattened_list.append((link[KEY], link[VALUE]))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Run this project's tests. Usage: tools/test [paths or pytest/node arguments].

With no arguments it runs the project's visible test suite. It stops after 50 seconds and says so, because the
sandbox kills any command at 60 seconds and reports only exit code 1.
"""
import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

LIMIT_S = 50
TOOLS = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
WORK = TOOLS.parent
REPO = WORK / "repo"
task = json.loads((TOOLS / "task.json").read_text())


def env():
    tmp = WORK / ".tmp"
    tmp.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    out = dict(os.environ, TMPDIR=str(tmp), PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1", PYTHONHASHSEED="0", PYTHONUTF8="1", TZ="UTC")
    paths = [str(REPO / p) for p in task.get("pythonpath", ".").split(":")]
    out["PYTHONPATH"] = os.pathsep.join([str(TOOLS / "pylib"), *paths])
    return out


def run(cmd):
    try:
        return subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=REPO, env=env(), timeout=LIMIT_S).returncode
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        print(f"TIMEOUT after {LIMIT_S}s: run fewer tests at once, for example one test file.")
        return 124


def python_tests(args):
    cmd = [sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider", "--continue-on-collection-errors", "--tb=short", *task.get("pytest_args", [])]
    cmd += [f"--deselect={t}" for t in task.get("deselect", [])]
    cmd += [f"--deselect={p}" for p in task.get("ignore", [])]  # not --ignore: a conftest hook can overrule it
    return run(cmd + (args or task.get("targets", [])))


def node_tests(args):
    excluded = tuple(task.get("test_exclude", []))
    files = args or sorted(
        str(p.relative_to(REPO))
        for root in task["test_paths"]
        for p in (REPO / root).rglob("*.js")
        if not str(p.relative_to(REPO)).startswith(excluded)
    )
    failed = 0
    for rel in files:
        try:
            proc = subprocess.run(["node", rel], cwd=REPO, env=env(), capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=LIMIT_S)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            print(f"TIMEOUT after {LIMIT_S}s: {rel}")
            failed += 1
            continue
        if proc.returncode:
            failed += 1
            lines = [l for l in proc.stdout.splitlines() if "not ok" in l]
            print(f"FAILED {rel}\n" + "\n".join(lines[:15]) + (proc.stderr[-400:] if not lines else ""))
    print(f"{len(files) - failed} of {len(files)} test files passed")
    return 1 if failed else 0


sys.exit(node_tests(sys.argv[1:]) if task["language"] == "js" else python_tests(sys.argv[1:]))

def _test_linkage(dll, max_count=10000, prev_idx=0, next_idx=1):
    """A function to test basic invariants of doubly-linked lists (with
    links made of Python lists).

    1. Test that the list is not longer than a certain length
    2. That the forward links (indicated by `next_idx`) correspond to
    the backward links (indicated by `prev_idx`).

    The `dll` parameter is the root/anchor link of the list.
    """
    start = cur = dll
    i = 0
    prev = None
    while 1:
        if i > max_count:
            raise Exception("did not return to anchor link after %r rounds"
                            % max_count)
        if prev is not None and cur is start:
            break
        prev = cur
        cur = cur[next_idx]
        if cur[prev_idx] is not prev:
            raise Exception('prev_idx does not point to prev at i = %r' % i)
        i += 1

    return True

`OrderedMultiDict == dict` is True even when the values differ

When I compare an `OrderedMultiDict` with a regular dict, only the keys seem to matter. If the keys line up, `==` says the two are equal even when the values are completely different.

from boltons.dictutils import OrderedMultiDict

from boltons.urlutils import QueryParamDict

params == {'x': 'other'}    # True, expected False
```

I expected `==` to be `False` as soon as a value differs, and `True` only when both the keys and the values match.

## Bug report

IndexedSet slices go wrong once something has been removed

`IndexedSet` is meant to support list-style slicing, but after I take an element out of the set, slices come back with the wrong items. Nothing raises; I just get bad data back.

```python
from boltons.setutils import IndexedSet

s = IndexedSet('abcdefghij')
s.remove('c')    # a b d e f g h i j

list(s[2:5])     # got ['e', 'f', 'g'], expected ['d', 'e', 'f']
list(s[-2:])     # got ['j'], expected ['i', 'j']
```

Rebuilding the set from its remaining items makes the slices correct again. I expected removals not to matter: a slice should match the same slice of a freshly built set with the same items, and forward slices should line up with `list(s)`.

Indexing and `pop` have a related problem: out-of-range negative positions should raise `IndexError` like a list, but `s[-10]` returns `'j'` and `s.pop(-15)` removes `'e'`.

    Whereas a :class:`set` keeps track of what it contains, a
    `complement set
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complement_(set_theory)>`_ keeps
    track of what it does *not* contain. For example, look what
    happens when we intersect a normal set with a complement set::

    >>> list(set(range(5)) & complement(set([2, 3])))
    [0, 1, 4]

    We get the everything in the left that wasn't in the right,
    because intersecting with a complement is the same as subtracting
    a normal set.

    Args:
        wrapped (set): A set or any other iterable which should be
           turned into a complement set.

    All set methods and operators are supported by complement sets,
    between other :func:`complement`-wrapped sets and/or regular
    :class:`set` objects.

    the set, functionality based on set contents is unavailable:
    :func:`len`, :func:`iter` (and for loops), and ``.pop()``. But a
    complement set can always be turned back into a regular set by
    complementing it again:

    >>> s = set(range(5))
    >>> complement(complement(s)) == s
    True

    .. note::

       An empty complement set corresponds to the concept of a
       `universal set <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_set>`_
       from mathematics.

    Complement sets by example
    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

    Many uses of sets can be expressed more simply by using a
    complement. Rather than trying to work out in your head the proper
    way to invert an expression, you can just throw a complement on
    the set. Consider this example of a name filter::

        >>> class NamesFilter(object):
        ...    def __init__(self, allowed):
        ...        self._allowed = allowed
        ...
        ...    def filter(self, names):
        ...        return [name for name in names if name in self._allowed]
        >>> NamesFilter(set(['alice', 'bob'])).filter(['alice', 'bob', 'carol'])

    We could try to enumerate all of the expected names::

    object is changed to filter ``['alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'dan']``?

    on this piece of code?  They cannot tell whether the purpose
    of the large allowed set was "allow everything", or if 'dan'
    was excluded for some subtle reason.

    A complement set lets the programmer intention be expressed
    succinctly and directly::

    the intention.

def test_iset_slice_after_removal():
    # PR #423: slice bounds were mapped into item_list space while islice

    # slices over-count.
    x = IndexedSet(range(10))

    assert list(x[1:4]) == [1, 3, 4]

    assert list(x[2:-1]) == [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
    assert isinstance(x[1:4], IndexedSet)


def test_iset_slice_agreement():
    # Slicing must not depend on dead slots: a set with removals must slice
    # identically to a freshly-built set with the same contents (all steps,
    # including the reversed-window negative-step semantics), and positive
    # steps must match list slicing exactly.
    bounds = (None, -12, -9, -5, -1, 0, 1, 4, 8, 9, 12)
    steps = (None, 1, 2, 3, -1, -2, -3)
    for pops in ([], [2], [0, 1, 2], [7, 8, 9], [0, 3, 6, 9], [1, 2, 5, 6]):
        iset = IndexedSet(range(10))
        for p in pops:
            iset.discard(p)
        fresh = IndexedSet(iset)  # same contents, no dead slots
        ref = list(iset)
        for start in bounds:
            for stop in bounds:
                for step in steps:
                    s = slice(start, stop, step)
                    assert list(iset[s]) == list(fresh[s]), (pops, s)
                    if step is None or step > 0:
                        assert list(iset[s]) == ref[s], (pops, s)

## Bug report

backoff_iter crashes on factor=1.0 when count is left out

`backoff_iter` rejects a `factor` below 1.0 with a `ValueError`, so 1.0 looks like valid input. But if I pass exactly 1.0 and leave out `count`, it dies with an unhandled error:

```python
from boltons.iterutils import backoff_iter

list(backoff_iter(2.0, 30.0, factor=1.0))
# ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
```

Giving an explicit `count` works and produces a flat sequence:

```python
list(backoff_iter(2.0, 30.0, count=4, factor=1.0))
# [2.0, 2.0, 2.0, 2.0]
```

A value the function's own validation lets through shouldn't end in a raw `ZeroDivisionError`. A flat sequence can never climb to a larger `stop`, so no count can be worked out here, and I expected a descriptive `ValueError` instead.

    """Generates a sequence of geometrically-increasing floats, suitable

    ecosystem.

    >>> list(backoff_iter(1.0, 10.0, count=5))
    [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 10.0]
    >>> list(backoff_iter(1.0, 10.0, count=8))
    [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0]

          try:
              res = network_call()
              break
          except Exception as e:
              log(e)
              time.sleep(timeout)

    An enhancement for large-scale systems would be to add variation,
    or *jitter*, to timeout values. This is done to avoid a thundering
    herd on the receiving end of the network call.

    Finally, for *count*, the special value ``'repeat'`` can be passed to
    continue yielding indefinitely.

    Args:

        start (float): Positive number for baseline.
        stop (float): Positive number for maximum.
        count (int): Number of steps before stopping
            iteration. Defaults to the number of steps between *start* and
            *stop*. Pass the string, `'repeat'`, to continue iteration
            indefinitely.
        factor (float): Rate of exponential increase. Defaults to `2.0`,
            e.g., `[1, 2, 4, 8, 16]`.
        jitter (float): A factor between `-1.0` and `1.0`, used to
            uniformly randomize and thus spread out timeouts in a distributed

            backoff curve as a maximum, negative values use the curve as a

    stop = float(stop)
    factor = float(factor)
    if start < 0.0:

    if factor < 1.0:

import json
import os
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

LIMIT_S = 50
TOOLS = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
WORK = TOOLS.parent
REPO = WORK / "repo"
task = json.loads((TOOLS / "task.json").read_text())


def env():
    tmp = WORK / ".tmp"
    tmp.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    out = dict(os.environ, TMPDIR=str(tmp), PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE="1", PYTHONHASHSEED="0", PYTHONUTF8="1", TZ="UTC")
    paths = [str(REPO / p) for p in task.get("pythonpath", ".").split(":")]
    out["PYTHONPATH"] = os.pathsep.join([str(TOOLS / "pylib"), *paths])
    return out


def run(cmd):
    try:
        return subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=REPO, env=env(), timeout=LIMIT_S).returncode
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        print(f"TIMEOUT after {LIMIT_S}s: run fewer tests at once, for example one test file.")
        return 124


def python_tests(args):
    cmd = [sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider", "--continue-on-collection-errors", "--tb=short", *task.get("pytest_args", [])]
    cmd += [f"--deselect={t}" for t in task.get("deselect", [])]
    cmd += [f"--deselect={p}" for p in task.get("ignore", [])]  # not --ignore: a conftest hook can overrule it
    return run(cmd + (args or task.get("targets", [])))


def node_tests(args):
    excluded = tuple(task.get("test_exclude", []))
    files = args or sorted(
        str(p.relative_to(REPO))
        for root in task["test_paths"]
        for p in (REPO / root).rglob("*.js")
        if not str(p.relative_to(REPO)).startswith(excluded)
    )
    failed = 0
    for rel in files:
        try:
            proc = subprocess.run(["node", rel], cwd=REPO, env=env(), capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=LIMIT_S)
        except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
            print(f"TIMEOUT after {LIMIT_S}s: {rel}")
            failed += 1
            continue
        if proc.returncode:
            failed += 1
            lines = [l for l in proc.stdout.splitlines() if "not ok" in l]
            print(f"FAILED {rel}\n" + "\n".join(lines[:15]) + (proc.stderr[-400:] if not lines else ""))
    print(f"{len(files) - failed} of {len(files)} test files passed")

sys.exit(node_tests(sys.argv[1:]) if task["language"] == "js" else python_tests(sys.argv[1:]))

def backoff(start, stop, count=None, factor=2.0, jitter=False):
    """Returns a list of geometrically-increasing floating-point numbers,
    suitable for usage with `exponential backoff`_. Exactly like
    :func:`backoff_iter`, but without the ``'repeat'`` option for
    *count*. See :func:`backoff_iter` for more details.

def backoff(start, stop, count=None, factor=2.0, jitter=False):
    """Returns a list of geometrically-increasing floating-point numbers,
    suitable for usage with `exponential backoff`_. Exactly like
    :func:`backoff_iter`, but without the ``'repeat'`` option for
    *count*. See :func:`backoff_iter` for more details.

    .. _exponential backoff: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_backoff

    >>> backoff(1, 10)
    [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 10.0]
    """
    if count == 'repeat':
        raise ValueError("'repeat' supported in backoff_iter, not backoff")
    return list(backoff_iter(start, stop, count=count,
                             factor=factor, jitter=jitter))


def backoff_iter(start, stop, count=None, factor=2.0, jitter=False):
    """Generates a sequence of geometrically-increasing floats, suitable
    for usage with `exponential backoff`_. Starts with *start*,
    increasing by *factor* until *stop* is reached, optionally
    stopping iteration once *count* numbers are yielded. *factor*
    defaults to 2. In general retrying with properly-configured
    backoff creates a better-behaved component for a larger service
    ecosystem.

    .. _exponential backoff: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_backoff

    >>> list(backoff_iter(1.0, 10.0, count=5))
    [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 10.0]
    >>> list(backoff_iter(1.0, 10.0, count=8))
    [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0, 10.0]
    >>> list(backoff_iter(0.25, 100.0, factor=10))
    [0.25, 2.5, 25.0, 100.0]

    A simplified usage example:

    .. code-block:: python

      for timeout in backoff_iter(0.25, 5.0):
          try:
              res = network_call()
              break
          except Exception as e:
              log(e)
              time.sleep(timeout)

    An enhancement for large-scale systems would be to add variation,
    or *jitter*, to timeout values. This is done to avoid a thundering
    herd on the receiving end of the network call.

    Finally, for *count*, the special value ``'repeat'`` can be passed to
    continue yielding indefinitely.

    Args:

        start (float): Positive number for baseline.
        stop (float): Positive number for maximum.
        count (int): Number of steps before stopping
            iteration. Defaults to the number of steps between *start* and
            *stop*. Pass the string, `'repeat'`, to continue iteration
            indefinitely.
        factor (float): Rate of exponential increase. Defaults to `2.0`,
            e.g., `[1, 2, 4, 8, 16]`.
        jitter (float): A factor between `-1.0` and `1.0`, used to
            uniformly randomize and thus spread out timeouts in a distributed
            system, avoiding rhythm effects. Positive values use the base
            backoff curve as a maximum, negative values use the curve as a
            minimum. Set to 1.0 or `True` for a jitter approximating
            Ethernet's time-tested backoff solution. Defaults to `False`.

    """
    start = float(start)
    stop = float(stop)
    factor = float(factor)
    if start < 0.0:
        raise ValueError('expected start >= 0, not %r' % start)
    if factor < 1.0:
        raise ValueError('expected factor >= 1.0, not %r' % factor)
    if stop == 0.0:
        raise ValueError('expected stop >= 0')
    if stop < start:
        raise ValueError('expected stop >= start, not %r' % stop)
    if count is None:
        if factor == 1.0:
            if start == stop:
                count = 1
            elif not start and stop <= 1.0:
                # a zero start bumps to 1 (clamped to stop) after the
                # first yield, so stop is reached on the second step
                count = 2
            else:
                raise ValueError(
                    'cannot infer count: factor of 1.0 produces a flat'
                    ' sequence which cannot climb to a larger stop'
                    ' (start=%r, stop=%r); pass count explicitly'
                    % (start, stop))
        else:
            denom = start if start else 1
            count = 1 + math.ceil(math.log(stop/denom, factor))
            count = count if start else count + 1
    if count != 'repeat' and count < 0:
        raise ValueError('count must be positive or "repeat", not %r' % count)
    if jitter:
        jitter = float(jitter)
        if not (-1.0 <= jitter <= 1.0):
            raise ValueError('expected jitter -1 <= j <= 1, not: %r' % jitter)

    cur, i = start, 0
    while count == 'repeat' or i < count:
        if not jitter:
            cur_ret = cur
        elif jitter:
            cur_ret = cur - (cur * jitter * random.random())
        yield cur_ret
        i += 1
        if cur == 0:
            cur = 1
        elif cur < stop:
            cur *= factor
        if cur > stop:
            cur = stop
    return

## Bug report

Passing a generator to OrderedMultiDict.addlist leaves the dict in a broken state

The docs for `addlist` say iterables work, but if I hand it a one-shot iterator such as a generator, the dict ends up inconsistent.

```python
from boltons.dictutils import OrderedMultiDict

omd = OrderedMultiDict()
omd.addlist('k', (n * 2 for n in range(3)))

omd.getlist('k')   # [], expected [0, 2, 4]
omd.get('k')       # IndexError, expected 4
```

`repr(omd)` still shows the values, so the dict disagrees with itself. With an empty generator, `len(omd)` is 1 while `keys()` is empty and `'k' in omd` is `True`. `QueryParamDict` in `boltons.urlutils` has the same problem.

I expected a one-shot iterable to behave exactly like the equivalent list: all values stored and retrievable, and an empty one adding nothing.

While showing file sizes in a dashboard with `humanize.naturalsize`, I noticed that values sitting just under a unit boundary come out looking wrong. The number rounds up, but the unit doesn't move with it:

```python
>>> from humanize import naturalsize
>>> naturalsize(999_960)
'1000.0 kB'
>>> naturalsize(999_980_000)
'1000.0 MB'

from __future__ import annotations

from math import log

from humanize.i18n import _gettext as _

    Non-GNU modes are compatible with jinja2's `filesizeformat` filter.

        '3.0 MB'
        >>> naturalsize(300, False, True)
        '300B'
        >>> naturalsize(3000, False, True)

        '2.9 KiB'

        '30000.0 QB'
        >>> naturalsize(-4096, True)

        format (str): Custom formatter.

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from math import log

from humanize.i18n import _gettext as _

suffixes = {
    "decimal": (
        "kB",
        "MB",
        "GB",
        "TB",
        "PB",
        "EB",
        "ZB",
        "YB",
        "RB",
        "QB",
    ),
    "binary": (
        "KiB",
        "MiB",
        "GiB",
        "TiB",
        "PiB",
        "EiB",
        "ZiB",
        "YiB",
        "RiB",
        "QiB",
    ),
    "gnu": "KMGTPEZYRQ",
}


def naturalsize(
    value: float | str,
    binary: bool = False,
    gnu: bool = False,
    format: str = "%.1f",
) -> str:
    """Format a number of bytes like a human-readable filesize (e.g. 10 kB).

    By default, decimal suffixes (kB, MB) are used.

    Non-GNU modes are compatible with jinja2's `filesizeformat` filter.

    Examples:
        ```pycon
        >>> naturalsize(3000000)
        '3.0 MB'
        >>> naturalsize(300, False, True)
        '300B'
        >>> naturalsize(3000, False, True)
        '2.9K'
        >>> naturalsize(3000, False, True, "%.3f")
        '2.930K'
        >>> naturalsize(3000, True)
        '2.9 KiB'
        >>> naturalsize(10**28)
        '10.0 RB'
        >>> naturalsize(10**34 * 3)
        '30000.0 QB'
        >>> naturalsize(-4096, True)
        '-4.0 KiB'

        ```

    Args:
        value (int, float, str): Integer to convert.
        binary (bool): If `True`, uses binary suffixes (KiB, MiB) with base
            2<sup>10</sup> instead of 10<sup>3</sup>.
        gnu (bool): If `True`, the binary argument is ignored and GNU-style
            (`ls -sh` style) prefixes are used (K, M) with the 2**10 definition.
        format (str): Custom formatter.

    Returns:
        str: Human readable representation of a filesize.
    """
    if gnu:
        suffix = suffixes["gnu"]
    elif binary:
        suffix = suffixes["binary"]
    else:
        suffix = suffixes["decimal"]

    base = 1024 if (gnu or binary) else 1000
    bytes_ = float(value)
    abs_bytes = abs(bytes_)

    if abs_bytes == 1 and not gnu:
        return _("%d Byte") % int(bytes_)

    if abs_bytes < base:
        return f"{int(bytes_)}B" if gnu else _("%d Bytes") % int(bytes_)

    exp = int(min(log(abs_bytes, base), len(suffix)))
    space = "" if gnu else " "
    scaled = bytes_ / (base**exp)

    # The formatted number can round up to the base (e.g. "1000.0 kB").
    # When that happens the unit must move up with it, unless we are
    # already at the largest unit.
    while exp < len(suffix):
        magnitude = _displayed_magnitude(format, scaled)
        if magnitude is None or magnitude < base:
            break
        exp += 1
        scaled = bytes_ / (base**exp)

    ret: str = format % scaled + space + _(suffix[exp - 1])
    return ret


_FORMATTED_NUMBER = re.compile(r"[-+]?(?:\d+(?:\.\d*)?|\.\d+)(?:[eE][-+]?\d+)?")


def _displayed_magnitude(format: str, value: float) -> float | None:
    """Absolute number as ``format`` renders ``value``, or ``None``.

    ``None`` means the formatted text does not expose a parseable number,
    in which case the exponent must be left alone.
    """
    try:
        rendered = format % value
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return None
    match = _FORMATTED_NUMBER.search(rendered)
    if match is None:
        return None
    try:
        return abs(float(match.group()))
    except ValueError:
        return None

`humanize.metric` sometimes prints one digit more than `precision` asks for. With the default of 3 I expect three significant figures, but a value that rounds up past a power of ten gets four:

```python
>>> import humanize
>>> humanize.metric(9996)
'10.00 k'
>>> humanize.metric(99960)
'100.0 k'
>>> humanize.metric(9.9996)
'10.00'
```

def metric(value: float, unit: str = "", precision: int = 3) -> str:
    """Return a value with a metric SI unit-prefix appended.

    Examples:
        ```pycon
        >>> metric(1500, "V")
        '1.50 kV'
        >>> metric(2e8, "W")
        '200 MW'
        >>> metric(220e-6, "F")
        '220 μF'
        >>> metric(1e-14, precision=4)
        '10.00 f'

        ```

    The unit prefix is always chosen so that non-significant zero digits are required.
    i.e. `123,000` will become `123k` instead of `0.123M` and `1,230,000` will become
    `1.23M` instead of `1230K`. For numbers that are either too huge or too tiny to
    represent without resorting to either leading or trailing zeroes, it falls back to
    `scientific()`.
    ```pycon
    >>> metric(1e40)
    '1.00 x 10⁴⁰'

    ```

    Args:
        value (int, float): Input number.
        unit (str): Optional base unit.
        precision (int): The number of digits the output should contain.

    Returns:
        str:
    """
    import math

    if not math.isfinite(value):
        return _format_not_finite(value)
    exponent = math.floor(math.log10(abs(value))) if value != 0 else 0

    if exponent >= 33 or exponent < -30:
        return scientific(value, precision - 1) + unit

    old_bucket = exponent // 3 * 3
    value /= 10**old_bucket
    digits = int(max(0, precision - exponent % 3 - 1))
    if exponent < 30 and round(abs(value), digits) >= 1000:
        exponent += 3 - exponent % 3
        new_bucket = exponent // 3 * 3
        value /= 10 ** (new_bucket - old_bucket)
        digits = int(max(0, precision - exponent % 3 - 1))

    if exponent >= 3:
        ordinal_ = "kMGTPEZYRQ"[exponent // 3 - 1]
    elif exponent < 0:
        ordinal_ = "mμnpfazyrq"[(-exponent - 1) // 3]
    else:
        ordinal_ = ""
    value_ = format(value, f".{digits}f")
    if not (unit or ordinal_) or unit in ("°", "′", "″"):
        space = ""
    else:
        space = " "

    return f"{value_}{space}{ordinal_}{unit}"

I bump prereleases with `semver.inc`, passing a dot-separated identifier so the version keeps its two-part tag. The counter never moves. Whatever number the version is on, it goes back to zero:

```js
const semver = require('semver')
semver.inc('5.2.0-rc.next.3', 'prerelease', 'rc.next')
// got:      5.2.0-rc.next.0
// expected: 5.2.0-rc.next.4
```

If I leave the identifier out, the number goes up as it should:

```js
semver.inc('5.2.0-rc.next.3', 'prerelease') // 5.2.0-rc.next.4
```

The version already has that identifier followed by a counter, so I expected the counter to go up, not restart from zero.

1. `id=null/undefined` + `base=false` rows: current THROWS 'identifier is empty' but my old didn't emulate that check — that check exists at top of inc() in BOTH old and new (unchanged code, `if (release.startsWith('pre'))`). My reconstruction just omitted it. Noise.

2. strict-mode '01' identifier rows: current THROWS 'invalid identifier: 01' — validation unchanged → old ALSO threw. My old omitted validation. Noise.

3. `1.2.3-01` strict input: current THROWS 'Invalid Version' — constructor unchanged. Noise.

4. `[true, ...]` (loose) rows with id='01': current vs old genuinely differ: e.g. loose `['1.2.3-0', 'prerelease', '01']` → current `1.2.3-1.0`, old `1.2.3-01.0`. And loose `['1.2.3-alpha.1','prerelease','01']` → current '1.2.3-1.0' vs old '1.2.3-01.0' — wait, interesting: current gives '1.2.3-1.0' — reset numberified '01'→1.

So the ONLY real behavioral differences for single-part identifiers are loose-mode leading-zero identifiers: old emitted the raw identifier ('01'), new emits numberified ('1').

Hmm — BUT: notice the constructor itself normalizes: parse('1.2.3-01.0', loose) → version '1.2.3-1.0'. And `parse('1.2.3-01', loose)` → version '1.2.3-1'?? Earlier test: `parse 01.0 -> 1.2.4-1.0`. So old output '1.2.4-01.0' was NOT the normalized `.version` — meaning old `inc()` returned a raw version string that differs from its own parse-normalized form. Actually wait — in old code, `this.raw = this.format()` where format joins this.prerelease — with old reset ['01', 0] → '01.0' → raw '1.2.4-01.0'. And `.version` also '01.0'. Then parse('1.2.4-01.0', loose).version → '1.2.4-1.0'. So old was internally inconsistent (inc output ≠ parse(inc output)).

New: '1.2.4-1.0' — consistent with parse. So new is arguably a FIX for that oddity — but it IS a single-part behavior change... However — hold on: is this actually OLD behavior? Old reset = [identifier, base] per description — yes raw '01'.

Hmm, but is this deviation worth reporting as a "problem"? The review's job: flag concrete regressions. This one:
- Input: `new SemVer('1.2.3', {loose:true}).inc('prerelease', '01')`

## Bug report

Tilde range with no patch number misses prereleases under includePrerelease

With `includePrerelease` turned on, a tilde range that leaves out the patch number doesn't match a prerelease of the first version in the range. The docs say `~3.4` means the same as `3.4.x`, and the x-range and caret forms both match it.

```js
const semver = require('semver')
const opts = { includePrerelease: true }
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '3.4.*', opts)   // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '>=3.4.*', opts) // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '^3.4.*', opts)  // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '~3.4.*', opts)  // false
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '~3.4', opts)    // false
```

I expected the last two to return `true` as well, so a tilde range behaves like the x-range it is documented to equal.

Unpack it first: `mkdir -p work out && tar -xzf uploads/node-semver-512-tilde.tar.gz -C work`. The project is then in `work/repo`.

An attempt is void if it fetches this project's code or its fix from the network, or reads another copy of this library on this machine.

## Bug report

Tilde range with no patch number misses prereleases under includePrerelease

With `includePrerelease` turned on, a tilde range that leaves out the patch number doesn't match a prerelease of the first version in the range. The docs say `~3.4` means the same as `3.4.x`, and the x-range and caret forms both match it.

```js
const semver = require('semver')
const opts = { includePrerelease: true }
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '3.4.*', opts)   // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '>=3.4.*', opts) // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '^3.4.*', opts)  // true
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '~3.4.*', opts)  // false
semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '~3.4', opts)    // false
```

I expected the last two to return `true` as well, so a tilde range behaves like the x-range it is documented to equal.

semver.satisfies('3.4.0-beta', '3.4.0 - 3.4', o)     // true   (expands to >=3.4.0-0 <3.5.0-0)

A failing case: the suite has no assertion that fails if the patch is reverted.

## Bug report

`semver.subset` returns false for a prerelease caret range inside another one

`semver.subset(a, b)` should return `true` when every version allowed by `a` is also allowed by `b`. That doesn't hold for caret ranges that start on prereleases of the same version:

```js
const semver = require('semver')
semver.subset('^6.3.0-rc.5', '^6.3.0-rc.4') // false
```

Everything `^6.3.0-rc.5` accepts, such as 6.3.0-rc.5, 6.3.0-rc.6 and later versions below 7.0.0, is accepted by `^6.3.0-rc.4` too, which only adds 6.3.0-rc.4 on top. So I expected `true` here.

## Bug report

`semver.coerce` cuts off prerelease identifiers that begin with a digit

I call `semver.coerce` with `{ includePrerelease: true }` on nightly version strings that end in a commit hash. When the hash starts with a digit, everything after the leading digits is lost:

```js
const semver = require('semver')
const opts = { includePrerelease: true }
semver.coerce('2.3.1-nightly.7f3c', opts).version
// got 2.3.1-nightly.7, expected 2.3.1-nightly.7f3c
semver.coerce('2.3.1-nightly.4821.9e1d', opts).version
// got 2.3.1-nightly.4821.9, expected 2.3.1-nightly.4821.9e1d
```

Identifiers that are all digits, or that start with a letter, such as `2.3.1-nightly.4821` or `2.3.1-nightly.a7f3`, come through intact. I expected the whole identifier to survive.
